{{Short description|Matrix whose entries are integers}}
In [[mathematics]], an '''integer matrix''' is a [[matrix (mathematics)|matrix]] whose entries are all [[integer]]s. Examples include  [[binary matrix|binary matrices]], the [[zero matrix]], the [[matrix of ones]], the [[identity matrix]], and the [[adjacency matrix|adjacency matrices]] used in [[graph theory]], amongst many others. Integer matrices find frequent application in [[combinatorics]].

==Examples==
:<math>\left(\begin{array}{cccr} 5 & 2 & 6 & 0\\ 4 & 7 & 3 & 8\\ 5 & 9 & 0 & 4\\ 3 & 1 & 0 & \!\!\!-3\\ 9 & 0 & 2 & 1\end{array}\right)</math>&nbsp; &nbsp; and &nbsp; &nbsp; <math>\left(\begin{array}{ccc} 1 & 5 & 0\\ 0 & 9 & 2\\ 1 & 7 & 3\end{array}\right)</math>
are both examples of integer matrices.

==Properties==
[[invertible matrix|Invertibility]] of integer matrices is in general more numerically stable than that of non-integer matrices. The [[determinant]] of an integer matrix <math>M</math> is itself an integer, and the [[adjugate matrix]] of an integer matrix is also integer matrix. Thus, the determinant of an invertible integer matrix is <math>1</math> or <math>-1</math>, and hence where inverses exist they do not become excessively large (see [[condition number]]). Theorems from [[Matrix (mathematics)|matrix theory]] that infer properties from determinants thus avoid the traps induced by [[Ill-conditioned matrix|ill conditioned]] (''nearly'' zero determinant) [[real number|real]] or [[floating point]] valued matrices.

The inverse of an integer matrix <math>M</math> is again an integer matrix if and only if the determinant of <math>M</math> equals <math>1</math> or <math>-1</math>.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hanson |first=Robert |date=1982 |title=Integer Matrices Whose Inverses Contain Only Integers |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/3026530 |journal=The Two-Year College Mathematics Journal |volume=13 |issue=1 |pages=18–21 |doi=10.2307/3026530 |jstor=3026530 |issn=0049-4925|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Integer matrices of determinant <math>1</math> form the [[group (mathematics)|group]] <math>\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbf{Z})</math>, which has far-reaching applications in arithmetic and [[geometry]]. For <math>n=2</math>, it is closely related to the [[modular group]].

The intersection of the integer matrices with the [[orthogonal group]] is the group of [[signed permutation matrices]].

The [[characteristic polynomial]] of an integer matrix has integer coefficients. Since the [[eigenvalue]]s of a matrix are the [[root of a function|roots]] of this polynomial, the eigenvalues of an integer matrix are [[algebraic integer]]s. In dimension [[Abel–Ruffini theorem|less than 5]], they can thus be expressed by [[Nth root|radicals]] involving integers.

Integer matrices are sometimes called ''integral matrices'', although this use is discouraged.
